name: Kilby semiconductor phase-shift oscillator configuration
summary: Kilby built a working oscillator whose transistor, resistor and capacitor were all made from semiconductor material, the first demonstration of an integrated circuit.
description: Kilby’s semiconductor phase-shift oscillator combines a transistor, resistive elements and a distributed resistor-capacitor network with electrical connections; his 1958 germanium oscillators are early physical witnesses.
tier_reason: Retain1 for this oscillator configuration. Integrated circuits being absent at0 does not make every early demonstration the whole breakthrough. This is a scoped consequence judgement, not a reward for documentation or representation.
why: Electronics makers struggled to wire together ever more separate components, and Kilby looked for a way to make all of them from one semiconductor material.

date.label: 12 Sep 1958
date.basis: Museum dates the working oscillator to 12 September 1958.

events.statement: Kilby connected germanium transistor, capacitor and resistor elements with fine gold wires to make an oscillator.
events.caveats: Museum caption calls this a multi-chip oscillator. It is not labelled a monolithic silicon IC; later TI flip-flops require separate nodes.

evidence.locator: Original oscillator caption; paragraph beginning On September 12, 1958
evidence.supports: Germanium elements, wire connections and working oscillator.

date.basis: Date the patent was issued and published; original application filing does not establish public access.

events.statement: Kilby’s issued patent publicly disclosed a semiconductor phase-shift oscillator configuration.
events.scope: Patent Figs. 8a–8c depict a semiconductor phase-shift oscillator with transistor and distributed resistor–capacitor elements; Kilby later described the embodiment as basically his 1958 oscillator.
events.caveats: The patent does not identify the actual 1958 physical specimen or independently establish that its oscillator embodiment used germanium and gold wires; the related 1959 publicly announced flip-flop is a different circuit.

evidence.locator: Issue date and Figs. 8a–8c, oscillator description
evidence.supports: The issued patent discloses a semiconductor transistor and distributed RC phase-shift oscillator.

evidence.locator: pp. 650–652, Figure 2 and patent application discussion
evidence.supports: Kilby describes the 1958 germanium oscillator and says one patent embodiment was basically that design.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. Museum dates the working oscillator to 12 September 1958. Museum caption calls this a multi-chip oscillator. It is not labelled a monolithic silicon IC; later TI flip-flops require separate nodes. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.community: Semiconductor engineers and readers of issued United States patents
community_entry.rationale: The 1964 issued patent publicly describes the related oscillator configuration and predates the Nobel lecture; it does not conflate the 1959 flip-flop.
community_entry.proxy_reason: The issued patent supports public technical awareness of the broadly refined configuration, not sale, adoption, the exact first disclosure, or exhibition of the 1958 specimen.
community_entry.caveats: The patent does not identify the actual 1958 physical specimen or independently establish that its oscillator embodiment used germanium and gold wires; the related 1959 publicly announced flip-flop is a different circuit.

caveats: The 1964 patent’s oscillator embodiment is described by Kilby as basically the 1958 design; the patent does not establish that the identical 1958 physical specimen or all materials were publicly displayed.

links.statement: Kilby's circuit has no links. What did it draw on?
links.caveats: Evidence needed: Kilby's lecture and Texas Instruments records.
links.finding: Kilby’s oscillator used a germanium mesa p–n–p transistor and passive elements, while the Bell device used closely spaced point contacts. The sources establish a shared semiconductor family but not a direct contribution by this particular 1947 prototype to Kilby’s oscillator.
